Currently our release pipeline (in broad strokes) works like this:
1. we go oven each wheel and sdist uploading them to pulp
2. we create advisory

At the end of the pulp-upload task we provide an overview of what packages were skipped (were already in pulp), which were successfully uploaded and which failed. If any uploads fail, the task also fails and pipeline doesn’t progress to the next task of advisory creation.

This could lead to multiple issues with missing data / inconsistent data:

# Advisory creation is skipped which means any wheels/sdist that was successfully uploaded will have missing advisory data
# We could have cases where wheel was uploaded successfully but the sdist upload failed (see [this failed release|https://konflux-ui.apps.kflux-prd-rh03.nnv1.p1.openshiftapps.com/ns/rhtap-releng-tenant/applications/calunga-v2-index-main/pipelineruns/managed-n9258/logs] ) 

Maybe there are other cases.

The release pipeline needs to be more robust.

Change the linked line in int test yaml to {{and not (name.startswith('pytest_') and}} package name doesn’t start with pytest {{)}}

items.toString:
Let’s create a POC of release watcher.
Problem:
When we merge a PR in {{index}} repo, we expect konflux to build it, create snapshot, run tests and then run release pipeline to release the wheel. But when anything in this process goes wrong (for example one of the ITS fails some network fluke), the wheel is not released and we don’t get notified and we have a discrepancy between what is in our repo (what should be released) and what is actually released.

This POC should be able to watch this whole release process and initially send slack notifications for successfull/failed releases. 

Next steps would be AI analysis of those failures to see if it really is a fluke (and whe should re-trigger the release process), or whether it is legitimate failure, that requires Engineering attention.

items.fromString:
h2. Description

Red Hat operates two public-facing catalog properties serving the same broad mission: providing developers and platform teams with hardened, verifiable, supply-chain-secure software artifacts. images.redhat.com is the Red Hat Hardened Images catalog — a browsable index of minimalist, distroless container images built from source using Red Hat's Konflux trusted software factory, carrying SLSA Level 3 provenance, SBOMs, and CVE reporting. packages.redhat.com is the complementary catalog for software libraries, currently housing two distinct tenants: Red Hat Trusted Libraries, a curated index of security-hardened Python packages (with NPM and Java planned), and the Red Hat AI Python Index, a curated collection of Python packages for AI and ML workloads on Red Hat AI, organized by hardware target.

Both portals address the same market shift that Chainguard does in recognizing that pulling software from public registries without provenance guarantees represents an unacceptable supply chain risk. The goal of this feature is to close the experience gap between the two Red Hat properties and ensure that the catalog experience users encounter on packages.redhat.com is on par with what images.redhat.com delivers, while accounting for the distinct nature of each property and its tenants.

h2. Current State

images.redhat.com presents a card-based catalog of over 45 container images spanning more than 150 variants across product categories including languages and runtimes (Python, Node.js, Go, Java, .NET, Rust), databases (PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Valkey, Memcached), web services (NGINX, HAProxy, Caddy, Apache Tomcat), developer tools, and OS base runtimes. The catalog requires no authentication to browse. Each image detail view is organized into tabs: Overview (available streams, variants, usage guidance), Tags (all image tags with size and last-updated metadata, filterable by FIPS compliance), SBOM (full Software Bill of Materials for the selected tag), CVE Reporting (known vulnerabilities for the selected tag), Verify Build (image integrity attestation), and Containerfile (downloadable build definition). Tag selection supports multiple pinning strategies suited to different stability requirements. A "Request an image" call to action allows users to signal demand.

packages.redhat.com currently serves two tenants under a shared domain. The Trusted Libraries tenant provides a pip-compatible Python package index at packages.redhat.com/trusted-libraries/python — developers point pip at this URL and consume curated, source-built packages like NumPy, Pandas, and Flask without changing their toolchain. h2. Recommended Approach

Three options exist for how to structure the alignment.

The first is a unified experience applied across both tenants. This is the lowest engineering cost path and produces the most visual consistency, but it accepts that the AI tenant's metadata model and user needs will be shoe-horned into a UX designed for a different purpose. The risk is that AIPCC users encounter a catalog experience that foregrounds provenance and security metadata that is secondary to their actual decision-making criteria.

The second is a shared platform foundation with tenant-differentiated experiences above it. The design system, tokens, navigation patterns, and shared components are standardized across both tenants, but each tenant controls its own catalog landing page, detail page tab structure, and filtering model. Trusted Libraries adopts the images.redhat.com UX closely — category browsing, tabbed detail pages with SBOM and CVE tabs, FIPS-equivalent filtering, security-first information hierarchy. The AI tenant adopts the shared visual language and structure but presents a hardware-compatibility matrix, platform-specific version information, and an information hierarchy oriented toward AI workload requirements. This approach requires more design and engineering investment but produces experiences that are actually useful to each audience.

The third is a fully configurable tenant framework where the platform is built as a white-label catalog engine that each tenant configures independently. This is the most extensible option for future tenants and language ecosystems (NPM, Java) but carries the highest upfront cost and is probably premature given the current state of the platform.

The recommended starting point is the second option. The shared foundation ensures that packages.redhat.com reads as a coherent Red Hat property alongside images.redhat.com, and tenant-differentiated experiences above that foundation ensure that each tenant's catalog is actually useful to its users. This approach also positions the platform well for the planned expansion to NPM and Java packages under the Trusted Libraries tenant, which can be added without revisiting the tenant model.

h2. Scope of Work

This feature spans three layers of work that are interdependent and need to be sequenced accordingly.

The first is a backend investigation to establish what security metadata is currently being generated, stored, and made available via API for packages in both tenants. For Trusted Libraries specifically, this means determining whether SLSA provenance documents, signed build attestations, SBOMs, and CVE scan results are being produced by the Konflux pipeline today, in what format they are stored, and whether there is an existing API surface through which the frontend can retrieve them per package and per version. For the AI Python Index tenant, the equivalent question is whether hardware compatibility data and platform certification status is structured in a queryable way. This investigation will produce a gap analysis: what exists and can be surfaced immediately, and what requires new backend work before the UI can expose it.

The second is backend development to close any gaps identified in the investigation. If SBOM data is being generated but not exposed via API, the work is an API surface addition. If CVE scanning is not yet integrated, that is a more substantial addition. The scope here cannot be fully defined until the investigation is complete, but it should be treated as part of this feature rather than deferred to a separate one, since the UI work has limited value without the data to back it.

The third is the frontend and UX work: aligning the visual design language and interaction patterns of packages.redhat.com with images.redhat.com, building catalog browsing and discovery experiences for both tenants, and surfacing the security metadata on package detail pages in a way that is comparable to what images.redhat.com provides on image detail pages today.

h2. Acceptance Criteria

The visual design language of packages.redhat.com — typography, color, component styling, spacing, header, footer, and navigation — is consistent with images.redhat.com, such that a user navigating between both properties encounters a coherent Red Hat catalog experience.

The Trusted Libraries tenant presents a catalog landing and detail page experience that is substantively aligned with images.redhat.com: category-organized browsing, a tabbed detail view surfacing provenance, SBOM, and CVE data inline, and filtering that includes compliance-relevant dimensions.

Security metadata for Trusted Libraries packages — including at minimum SBOM contents, SLSA provenance, and CVE status — is accessible and readable on package detail pages without leaving the site.

The AI Python Index tenant shares the platform's visual foundation and navigation structure but presents an experience organized around its own information hierarchy: hardware target variants (CPU, CUDA, ROCm), platform compatibility, and framework-specific metadata.

The distinction between the two tenants is clear to users arriving at packages.redhat.com, including the difference in mission, content, and access requirements.

No existing functionality of either tenant is regressed. Both tenants meet WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility requirements.

h2. Definition of Ready

A backend investigation has been completed and a gap analysis is available covering: which security metadata artifacts are currently being generated per package in the Trusted Libraries pipeline, which are queryable via existing API, and which require new backend work before the UI can surface them.

The frontend architecture of packages.redhat.com has been confirmed, including the component library in use and the feasibility of the tenant-differentiated model described in the Recommended Approach section.

Agreement has been reached on how the two tenants are presented and distinguished at the packages.redhat.com entry point.

The design system shared with images.redhat.com has been confirmed, including any shared header and footer components.

h2. Open Questions and evaluations

What security metadata artifacts — SLSA provenance documents, build attestations, SBOMs, CVE scan results — are currently being generated by the Trusted Libraries Konflux pipeline, and are any of them exposed via an API the frontend can query today?

Revisit the UX exploration work done previously to improve the consistency of how tenant workflows behave, and compare/contrast with [images.redhat.com|http://images.redhat.com] - 

For the AI Python Index tenant, is hardware variant and platform compatibility data structured in a way that supports a rich detail page experience, or is it currently flat metadata?

Multi-tenant product model: Do we need to revisit? Does RHAI and Trusted Libraries present as two distinct products sharing a codebase, or one product with two modes? The answer drives how the header, navigation, and feature gating behave across the whole alignment effort — if they're distinct products, the chrome may need to feel different per tenant; if they're one product, a unified chrome is correct.                           

  NavigationPrimary per-tenant branding: The current header already swaps logos by domain (rhai.svg vs trusted-libraries.svg). Should the RHDS NavigationPrimary follow the same per-tenant pattern — different title/logo depending on which domain you're in — or standardize to a single "[http://packages.redhat.com|http://packages.redhat.com|smart-link] " brand at the top?                                                                    

RHAI distribution list UX: The AI Index has a distribution selection step (CPU/CUDA/ROCm hardware targets) with no equivalent anywhere on  
  [http://images.redhat.com|http://images.redhat.com|smart-link] . What UX pattern should this screen follow after alignment? Does it stay as a list, become a card grid, or get a hardware compatibility matrix?                                                                                                                     

  "Request Package" CTA scope: Should the engagement CTA in the header apply to Trusted Libraries (mirroring "Request Image" on [http://images.redhat.com|http://images.redhat.com|smart-link] ), or to RHAI?

  @rhds/elements + tsd-ui coexistence (resolved by Spike A0): Can @rhds/elements web components be added alongside the existing tsd-ui dependency in the Vite 7-built Pulp UI fork without CSS variable collisions or ESM interop failures? If not, the RHDS chrome swap needs a alternative approach.                                                                                                                      

  Security metadata API availability (resolved by Spike B0): Where are SBOM files and SLSA attestations stored for Trusted Libraries packages — Pulp Content API, OCI registry attachment, or Sigstore/Rekor? This determines whether the SBOM and Provenance tabs can call external APIs directly or need a server-side proxy.
